# Skill: subagent-driven-development

# Subagent-Driven Development

Execute plan by dispatching a fresh implementer subagent per task, a task review (spec compliance + code quality) after each, and a broad whole-branch review at the end.

**Why subagents:** You delegate tasks to specialized agents with isolated context. By precisely crafting their instructions and context, you ensure they stay focused and succeed at their task. They should never inherit your session's context or history — you construct exactly what they need. This also preserves your own context for coordination work.

**Core principle:** Fresh subagent per task + task review (spec + quality) + broad final review = high quality, fast iteration

**Narration:** between tool calls, narrate at most one short line — the
ledger and the tool results carry the record.

**Continuous execution:** Do not pause to check in with your human partner between tasks. Execute all tasks from the plan without stopping. The only reasons to stop are the four named below, or all tasks complete. "Should I continue?" prompts and progress summaries waste their time — they asked you to execute the plan, so execute it.

**Rulings, not stalls.** A running plan does not wait on a human. Conflicts,
ambiguities, plan defects, a cap you would have asked to exceed — decide
them. The spec is the binding authority, the plan is its argument, and your
judgment settles what neither answers. Record every decision in the ledger as
`Ruling: <what you decided> — <why> — <what it costs if wrong>`, and keep
going. A wrong ruling costs rework your human partner can see and undo; a
session parked on a question costs their whole day and buys nothing.

Four things stop you, and only these: an irreversible or destructive
operation; a security-sensitive action; a side effect outside this worktree
that norms say you ask about first (a merge, a push to a shared branch, a
publish); and a plan so broken that every path forward is a guess. For those,
stop and ask.

## Setup

Ensure the work happens in an isolated workspace: use
superpowers:using-git-worktrees to create one or verify the existing one.
Never start implementation on a main/master branch without your human
partner's explicit consent.

Conversation memory does not survive compaction. In real sessions,
controllers that lost their place have re-dispatched entire completed task
sequences — the single most expensive failure observed. Track progress in
a ledger file, not only in todos.

- Each plan owns a workspace: at skill start, run this skill's
  `bash scripts/sdd-workspace PLAN_FILE` — it prints the plan's git-ignored
  directory (under `<repo-root>/.superpowers/sdd/`), home to
  every artifact for THIS plan: ledger, briefs, reports, review packages.
  Another plan's directory is never yours to read or write.
- Check for this plan's ledger at `<workspace>/progress.md`. If its first
  line names your plan file, tasks with a `Task <N>: complete` line are DONE
  — do not re-dispatch them; resume at the first task without one. A task
  whose last line is a fix round is mid-loop: resume the loop at the next
  round. A ledger whose first line names a different plan file — or a stray
  ledger at the old flat path `.superpowers/sdd/progress.md` — is another
  plan's progress: leave it in place and start your own, fresh.
- Create the ledger with its identity as the first line:
  `# SDD ledger — plan: <plan file path>`.
- The ledger is your recovery map: the commits it names exist in git even
  when your context no longer remembers creating them. After compaction,
  trust the ledger and `git log` over your own recollection.
- `git clean -fdx` will destroy the workspace (it's git-ignored scratch); if
  that happens, recover from `git log`.

Read the plan once, note its context and Global Constraints, and create a
todo per task. If the plan names a Spec, read that too: the spec is the
authority the plan argues from, and conflicts inside the plan resolve
against it. A plan with no reachable spec gets a ledger note saying so —
rulings made without one are provisional.

Before dispatching Task 1, scan the plan once for conflicts, writing down
what you checked as you check it:

- tasks that contradict each other or the plan's Global Constraints
- anything the plan explicitly mandates that the review rubric treats as a
  defect (a test that asserts nothing, verbatim duplication of a logic block)

The scan's output is a table, not a verdict. One row for every pair of tasks
that share a file or an interface: the two tasks, what one produces against
what the other consumes, and what you found. One row for every task: whether
its own text agrees with itself — the tests it specifies against the code it
specifies, the files it creates against the files it later touches. "The scan
is clean" without those rows is not a scan you ran.

Write the table to the ledger. Rule on everything you find before execution
begins — each finding against the plan text that mandates it — and record
each ruling in the ledger. If the scan is clean, proceed without comment.
Rule on each conflict it surfaces — the spec is the binding authority, the
plan is its argument — record the ruling beside its row, and dispatch
Task 1. The review loop remains the net for conflicts that only emerge from
implementation.

## Model Selection

Use the least powerful model that can handle each role to conserve cost and increase speed.

**Mechanical implementation tasks** (isolated functions, clear specs, 1-2 files): use a fast, cheap model. Most implementation tasks are mechanical when the plan is well-specified.

**Integration and judgment tasks** (multi-file coordination, pattern matching, debugging): use a standard model.

**Architecture and design tasks**: use the most capable available model.
The final whole-branch review is one of these — dispatch it on the most
capable available model, not the session default.

**Review tasks**: choose the model with the same judgment, scaled to the
diff's size, complexity, and risk. A small mechanical diff does not need the
most capable model; a subtle concurrency change does. Scoped re-reviews of
small fix diffs take a cheap-to-mid tier.

**Fix-loop escalation (rounds 4-5)**: use a model at least one tier above
the implementer that got stuck.

**Always specify the model explicitly when dispatching a subagent.** An
omitted model inherits your session's model — often the most capable and
most expensive — which silently defeats this section.

**Turn count beats token price.** Wall-clock and context cost scale with how
many turns a subagent takes, and the cheapest models routinely take 2-3× the
turns on multi-step work — costing more overall. Use a mid-tier model as the
floor for reviewers and for implementers working from prose descriptions.
When the task's plan text contains the complete code to write, the
implementation is transcription plus testing: use the cheapest tier for
that implementer. Single-file mechanical fixes also take the cheapest tier.

**Task complexity signals (implementation tasks):**
- Touches 1-2 files with a complete spec → cheap model
- Touches multiple files with integration concerns → standard model
- Requires design judgment or broad codebase understanding → most capable model

## The Task Loop

**Batch small same-shape work.** When the plan lists several tasks that are
each a small, independent edit of the same kind — the same one-line fix,
constant change, or field addition repeated across files — do not dispatch
one subagent per task. Compose ONE dispatch brief listing every file and
its change, send the whole batch to a single subagent, and review its diff
as one unit. Reserve one-dispatch-per-task for work that needs its own
judgment, its own tests, or its own review surface.

Everything you paste into a dispatch prompt — and everything a subagent
prints back — stays resident in your context for the rest of the session
and is re-read on every later turn. Hand artifacts over as files.

**Waiting on dispatched subagents:** never poll a wait interface with
short timeouts, and never sit in one silent, open-ended wait either.
While you have local work — ledger updates, packaging the next review,
reading reports — keep working; child results arrive on their own.
When you are genuinely idle, wait in bounded stretches (five to ten
minutes, where your platform allows), and between stretches post one
line of status and reconcile your live children: list them, and chase
any that finished without reporting. A bounded stretch keeps nearly
all of a long wait's efficiency while guaranteeing a stuck or lost
child is noticed within minutes, not at the end of the session.

### 1. Dispatch the implementer

Record BASE (`git rev-parse HEAD`) before dispatching — the review package
and fix-round diffs need it.

- **Task brief:** before dispatching an implementer, run this skill's
  `bash scripts/task-brief PLAN_FILE N` — it extracts the task's full text to a
  uniquely named file and prints the path. Compose the dispatch so the
  brief stays the single source of
  requirements. Your dispatch should contain: (1) one line on where this
  task fits in the project; (2) the brief path, introduced as "read this
  first — it is your requirements, with the exact values to use verbatim";
  (3) interfaces and decisions from earlier tasks that the brief cannot
  know; (4) your resolution of any ambiguity you noticed in the brief;
  (5) the report-file path and report contract. Exact values (numbers,
  magic strings, signatures, test cases) appear only in the brief. Never
  make a subagent read the whole plan file.
- **Report file:** name the implementer's report file after the brief
  (brief `…/task-N-brief.md` → report `…/task-N-report.md`) and put it in
  the dispatch prompt. The implementer writes the full report there and
  returns only status, commits, a one-line test summary, and concerns.
- A dispatch prompt describes one task, not the session's history. Do not
  paste accumulated prior-task summaries ("state after Tasks 1-3") into
  later dispatches — a real session's dispatch hit 42k chars of which 99%
  was pasted history. A fresh subagent needs its task, the interfaces it
  touches, and the global constraints. Nothing else.
- The dispatch carries the no-subagents contract (it is in the
  implementer template): the implementer never dispatches subagents —
  not helpers, and never a reviewer. Review arrives from you, after the
  report. In real sessions, every reviewer a worker spawned duplicated
  the task review the controller dispatched anyway — a full extra
  review seat per task.
- If an earlier task parked a finding in the area this task touches, carry
  a pointer to that ledger entry in the dispatch.
- Record the implementer's agent identity from the dispatch result —
  fix-loop rounds 1-3 resume this agent.
- Never dispatch multiple implementation subagents in parallel (conflicts).

Template: [implementer-prompt.md](implementer-prompt.md)

### 2. Handle the report

Implementer subagents report one of four statuses. Handle each appropriately:

**DONE:** Generate the review package (`bash scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE BASE HEAD`, from this skill's directory — it prints the unique file path it wrote; BASE is the commit you recorded before dispatching the implementer — never `HEAD~1`, which silently drops all but the last commit of a multi-commit task), then dispatch the task reviewer with the printed path.

**DONE_WITH_CONCERNS:** The implementer completed the work but flagged doubts. Read the concerns before proceeding. If the concerns are about correctness or scope, address them before review. If they're observations (e.g., "this file is getting large"), note them and proceed to review.

**NEEDS_CONTEXT:** The implementer needs information that wasn't provided. Provide the missing context and re-dispatch.

**BLOCKED:** The implementer cannot complete the task. Assess the blocker:
1. If it's a context problem, provide more context and re-dispatch with the same model
2. If the task requires more reasoning, re-dispatch with a more capable model
3. If the task is too large, break it into smaller pieces
4. If the plan itself is wrong, rule on the correction, ledger it, and re-dispatch with the ruling carried in the dispatch

**Never** ignore an escalation or force the same model to retry without changes. If the implementer said it's stuck, something needs to change.

If the implementer asks questions — before starting or mid-task — answer
clearly and completely, provide additional context if needed, and don't
rush it into implementation.

### 3. Review the task

Per-task reviews are task-scoped gates. The broad review happens once, at the
final whole-branch review. Never skip the task review, and never accept a
report missing either verdict — spec compliance AND task quality are both
required. Implementer self-review never replaces the task review; both are
needed.

- Hand the reviewer its diff as a file: run this skill's
  `bash scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE BASE HEAD` and pass the reviewer the file path
  it prints (or, without bash: `git log --oneline`, `git diff --stat`,
  and `git diff -U10` for the range, redirected to one uniquely named
  file). The output never enters your own context, and the reviewer sees
  the commit list, stat summary, and full diff with context in one Read
  call. Use the BASE you recorded before dispatching the implementer —
  never `HEAD~1`, which silently truncates multi-commit tasks. Never
  dispatch a task reviewer without a diff file.
- **Reviewer inputs:** the task reviewer gets three paths — the same brief
  file, the report file, and the review package — plus the global
  constraints that bind the task.
- The global-constraints block you hand the reviewer is its attention
  lens. Copy the binding requirements verbatim from the plan's Global
  Constraints section or the spec: exact values, exact formats, and the
  stated relationships between components ("same layout as X", "matches
  Y"). The reviewer's template already carries the process rules (YAGNI,
  test hygiene, review method) — the constraints block is for what THIS
  project's spec demands.
- Do not add open-ended directives like "check all uses" or "run race tests
  if useful" without a concrete, task-specific reason
- Do not ask a reviewer to re-run tests the implementer already ran on the
  same code — the implementer's report carries the test evidence
- Do not pre-judge findings for the reviewer — never instruct a reviewer to
  ignore or not flag a specific issue. If you believe a finding would be a
  false positive, let the reviewer raise it and adjudicate it in the review
  loop. If the prompt you are writing contains "do not flag," "don't treat X
  as a defect," "at most Minor," or "the plan chose" — stop: you are
  pre-judging, usually to spare yourself a review loop.
The task reviewer may report "⚠️ Cannot verify from diff" items — requirements
that live in unchanged code or span tasks. These do not block the rest of the
review, but you must resolve each one yourself before marking the task
complete: you hold the plan and cross-task context the reviewer
lacks. If you confirm an item is a real gap, treat it as a failed spec
review — it enters the fix loop with the other findings.

Template: [task-reviewer-prompt.md](task-reviewer-prompt.md)

### 4. The fix loop

The loop triggers when the review reports spec ❌, any Critical or Important
finding, or a ⚠️ item you confirmed as a real gap.

Before the loop starts, two routes leave it immediately:

- Record Minor findings in the progress ledger as you go
  (`Task <N>: minor (deferred): <one-liner>`), and point the final
  whole-branch review at that list so it can triage which must be fixed
  before merge. A roll-up nobody reads is a silent discard. Minor findings
  never enter the loop.
- A finding labeled plan-mandated — or any finding that conflicts with
  what the plan's text requires — is yours to rule on: weigh the finding
  against the plan text, decide with the spec as the binding authority, and
  ledger the ruling before you act on it. Do not dismiss the finding because
  the plan mandates it, and do not dispatch a fix that contradicts the plan
  without a recorded ruling.
Everything else enters the loop. A fix round is one fix dispatch plus one
scoped re-review. Five rounds maximum per task:

**Rounds 1-3 — resume the original implementer.** Send it the open findings
verbatim. Its context is intact: it knows the task, the code, and its own
choices. If your harness cannot send another message to a live subagent,
dispatch a fresh implementer carrying the brief path, the report-file path,
and the findings — the report file is the persistent memory either way.

**Rounds 4-5 — dispatch a fresh implementer on a more capable model** (per
Model Selection), with the brief path, the report-file path, the open
findings, and this framing: "A prior implementer attempted this task
[N] times; you own it now. Read the report file for what was tried." A loop
that survives three resumes usually means the implementer cannot see its
own problem — fresh eyes and a capability bump in one move.

**Every round, either way:** the implementer fixes, re-runs the tests
covering the amended code, appends its fix report to the same report file,
and returns the short contract. Before re-dispatching the reviewer, confirm
the fix report contains the covering tests, the command run, and the
output; dispatch the re-review once all three are present. Name the
covering test files in the fix message — a one-line fix does not need the
whole suite.

**The re-review is scoped.** Run `bash scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE FIX_BASE HEAD`
where FIX_BASE is the head the previous review saw, and dispatch
[re-review-prompt.md](re-review-prompt.md) with the findings list, the
brief, the report file, and the printed diff path. The re-reviewer verdicts
each finding ADDRESSED or NOT ADDRESSED and flags new breakage in the fix
diff only. New Critical/Important breakage in the fix diff joins the open
findings list. Out-of-scope observations go to the ledger as deferred
minors — they never extend the loop.

**After each round,** append to the ledger:
`Task <N>: fix round <R>/5 (<X> addressed, <Y> open — <finding one-liners>; commits <a7>..<b7>)`

Never fix findings yourself in the controller session — your context stays
clean for coordination, and controller fixes skip review.

**The breaker.** When round 5's re-review still leaves findings open, stop
dispatching. Adjudicate each open finding yourself — you hold the plan and
the cross-task context the reviewer lacks:

- **The reviewer is wrong, or the point is contestable:** park it —
  `Task <N>: parked — <finding> — Ruling: <why the code stands>`. The final
  review sees both sides.
- **Real, but nothing downstream builds on it:** park it the same way, with
  a ruling that says it's real and deferred.
- **Real and load-bearing** — a later task builds on it, or it reveals a
  plan defect: rule on the smallest change that unblocks the dependent work,
  ledger it as `Task <N>: Ruling: <finding> — <what you decided and why>`,
  and carry it into the next task's dispatch. Parking a structural failure
  silently lets every dependent task build on it. Stop only when the defect
  leaves every path forward a guess.

Adjudicate only at the cap. Adjudicating earlier to end a loop is
pre-judging with a different name. Every adjudication is a ledger entry —
a silent discard is forbidden.

### 5. Complete the task

When the review comes back clean — or every open finding is parked with a
ruling at the cap — append the completion line to the ledger in the same
message as your other bookkeeping:

- `Task <N>: complete (commits <base7>..<head7>, review clean)`
- `Task <N>: complete (commits <base7>..<head7>, <K> parked)` after a
  tripped breaker

Then mark the todo complete and move on. Never move to the next task while
the review has open Critical/Important issues that are neither fixed nor
parked-with-ruling at the cap.

## Final Review

The final whole-branch review gets a package too: run
`bash scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE MERGE_BASE HEAD` (MERGE_BASE = the commit the
branch started from, e.g. `git merge-base main HEAD`) and include the
printed path in the final review dispatch, so the final reviewer reads
one file instead of re-deriving the branch diff with git commands. Dispatch
on the most capable available model (see Model Selection), using
superpowers:requesting-code-review's
[code-reviewer.md](../requesting-code-review/code-reviewer.md). Point it at
the ledger's deferred-minor and parked lines so it can triage which must be
fixed before merge.

If the final whole-branch review returns findings, dispatch ONE fix subagent
with the complete findings list — not one fixer per finding.
Per-finding fixers each rebuild context and re-run suites; a real
session's final-review fix wave cost more than all its tasks combined.
Then run exactly one scoped re-review of the fix wave
(`bash scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE FIX_BASE HEAD` over the fix range,
[re-review-prompt.md](re-review-prompt.md)).
Adjudicate any residual findings as in the task loop's breaker: park with
rulings, or rule on the load-bearing ones and ledger what you decided. Only
the four classes above stop you here. There is no second fix wave —
residual load-bearing findings surface to your human partner when
finishing-a-development-branch presents the options.

## Finish

Before you delete anything, collect every ledger line containing `Ruling:` —
preflight rulings, parked findings, breaker adjudications, all of them — into
your final message under "Rulings I made", in the order you made them, each
with what it costs if wrong. The list is exhaustive: if the ledger holds a
ruling, the list holds it. That list is the only place the decisions you
took on your human partner's behalf reach them — they read it and rework
whatever you got wrong. A ruling that dies with the workspace was a decision
made in secret.

When the final whole-branch review is clean and its fixes are merged,
delete this plan's workspace (`rm -rf <workspace>`) — the git history is
the record now. Sibling directories belong to other plans; leave them
alone.

Use superpowers:finishing-a-development-branch.

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Close enough on spec compliance" | Reviewer found spec gaps = not done. Fix or hit the cap and adjudicate — those are the only exits. |
| "I'll fix it myself, dispatching is overhead" | Controller fixes pollute your context and skip review. Resume the implementer. |
| "One more round will converge" | Past the cap, rounds don't converge — the failure is structural. Adjudicate and route. |
| "The reviewer will just find something new anyway" | Scoped re-reviews verify fixes; they cannot wander. New findings on untouched code go to the ledger, not the loop. |
| "This finding is obviously wrong, I'll drop it" | You adjudicate only at the cap, and every ruling is a ledger entry. Silent discards are forbidden. |
| "The fix was small, skip the re-review" | Unreviewed fixes are how regressions land. Every round ends with a scoped re-review. |
| "Reviews slow the loop down" | The loop without reviews is just unverified churn. Reviews are the loop's brakes and steering. |
| "Ledger bookkeeping is overhead" | The ledger is what survives compaction. Controllers without one have re-dispatched entire completed task sequences. |
| "The implementer spawned its own reviewer — free extra assurance" | It's a duplicate seat reviewing the same diff; the task review is the gate. A worker-spawned reviewer is a defect to flag, not rigor. |

## Example Workflow


# Tether — plan d'implémentation Phase 0 + 1

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** Établir l'infrastructure mono-serveur + chaîne de build Android, puis livrer un client Tether capable de lister les sessions opencode de le serveur et de tenir une conversation en streaming depuis le Pixel.

**Architecture:** Un serveur opencode unique (`opencode-remote.service`, `0.0.0.0:4096`) sert le TUI du PC et le téléphone. L'app Kotlin/Compose parle l'API V2 en REST (`/api/*`) pour l'état et en SSE (`GET /api/event`) pour le direct. Un `EventReducer` transforme le flux d'événements en état de session ; la vérité vient toujours du REST, le flux ne sert qu'à l'instantané.

**Tech Stack:** Kotlin 2.0.x · Jetpack Compose (Material 3) · Hilt · Ktor client (okhttp engine + SSE) · kotlinx-serialization · multiplatform-markdown-renderer · Coil · Gradle version catalog. Plugin serveur : TypeScript (opencode V2).

**Spec:** `~/Projects/tether/docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-24-tether-design.md`

## Global Constraints

- **Licence : MIT.**
- **Appareil cible : Pixel 10 Pro XL (`pixel-de-test`), Android 17 / SDK 37, arm64-v8a.**
- **Aucune dépendance Play Services / Firebase / GMS.** Rédhibitoire sur GrapheneOS.
- **Jamais de PWA.** Application Android native Kotlin/Compose.
- **API opencode V2 uniquement** — toutes les routes sous `/api/*`. Les routes V1 renvoient `200 text/html` (fallback SPA) et **doivent être rejetées** : filtrer sur `Content-Type`.
- **L'appareil de test est sous Android 16+** → les règles de *foreground service* récentes s'appliquent (type déclaré, permissions).
- Palette : fonds `#0B0E11` / surfaces `#11151A` ; texte `#E6EDF3`, secondaire `#8B98A5` ; accent teal `#2DD4BF` ; alerte ambre `#FFB020`.
- Pas de Gson (doublon interdit). kotlinx-serialization seul.
- **Ne jamais lancer `opencode service set|restart|start` en synchrone depuis une session opencode active** : ça tue le service de fond et les sessions en cours. Toujours en détaché.

## Review Focus

Ces points sont implicites dans le spec et aucun test ne les couvre naturellement — ils sont chacun rattachés à une tâche ci-dessous.

1. **Un flux SSE qui renvoie du `text/html`** (fallback SPA V1) au lieu de `text/event-stream` — le client doit **échouer proprement et re-tenter**, jamais parser du HTML comme des événements (piège KTOR-9023).
2. **Une session ouverte pendant que le téléphone est hors-ligne**, puis reconnecté : l'état doit être **reconstruit depuis le REST**, pas complété par un flux tronqué (la règle « la vérité vient du REST »).
3. **Un événement SSE portant `data.sessionID`** (forme V2) : ne pas chercher `sessionID` à la racine ni dans `properties` — leçon du portage `ntfy-opencode`, vérifiée sur tour réel.
4. **Une réponse assistant arrivant en `content[]` typé et encodé** : ne pas supposer un modèle « message + parts » ; un type de contenu inconnu doit être **affiché en repli brut**, jamais jeter le message.
5. **Un `POST /prompt` qui réussit mais ne renvoie pas de message** (il renvoie un item d'inbox) : l'UI ne doit pas rester bloquée « en attente de réponse » si l'événement d'inbox n'arrive pas.

```kotlin
class OpenCodeClient(
    private val baseUrl: String,
    private val credentials: BasicAuthCredentials,
    private val http: HttpClient,
) {
    private fun url(path: String, location: String) = "$baseUrl$path?location%5Bdirectory%5D=$location"

    suspend fun info(): ServerInfo =
        http.get("$baseUrl/api/info") { auth() }.body()

    suspend fun sessions(location: String): List<Session> =
        http.get(url("/api/session", location)) { auth() }.body<DataEnvelope<Session>>().data

    suspend fun messages(sessionID: String, location: String): List<MessageDto> =
        http.get(url("/api/session/$sessionID/message", location)) { auth() }.body<DataEnvelope<MessageDto>>().data

    suspend fun prompt(sessionID: String, text: String, location: String): Unit =
        http.post(url("/api/session/$sessionID/prompt", location)) {
            auth()
            contentType(ContentType.Application.Json)
            setBody(PromptBody(text = text))
        }.body()

    // ⚠️ Le modèle se fixe à la CRÉATION de la session.
    suspend fun createSession(title: String, model: ModelRef, location: String): Session =
        http.post("$baseUrl/api/session") {
            auth()
            contentType(ContentType.Application.Json)
            setBody(CreateSessionBody(title = title, model = model, location = LocationBody(location)))
        }.body<DataEnvelope<Session>>().data.first()

    private fun HttpRequestBuilder.auth() { basicAuth("opencode", credentials.password) }
}
```

- [ ] **Step 3 : Implémenter**

`SseParser.kt` — parser **incrémental** (le réseau coupe les frames n'importe où), accumulation par `\n\n`, extraction des lignes `data:` (et `event:` s'il existe, **selon la capture réelle de Task 0.1**), gestion de `retry:` et `id:` :

```kotlin
class NotSseException(msg: String) : Exception(msg)

class SseParser {
    private val buffer = StringBuilder()

    fun feed(chunk: String): List<SseFrame> {
        buffer.append(chunk)
        val frames = mutableListOf<SseFrame>()
        while (true) {
            val idx = buffer.indexOf("\n\n")
            if (idx < 0) break
            val raw = buffer.substring(0, idx)
            buffer.delete(0, idx + 2)
            parseFrame(raw)?.let { frames += it }
        }
        return frames
    }

    private fun parseFrame(raw: String): SseFrame? {
        val data = raw.lineSequence()
            .filter { it.startsWith("data:") }
            .joinToString("\n") { it.removePrefix("data:").trimStart() }
        if (data.isEmpty()) return null
        val id = raw.lineSequence().firstOrNull { it.startsWith("id:") }?.removePrefix("id:")?.trim()
        return SseFrame(id = id, data = data)
    }

    companion object {
        fun requireEventStream(contentType: String?) {
            if (contentType == null || !contentType.startsWith("text/event-stream"))
                throw NotSseException("Content-Type inattendu : $contentType (fallback SPA ?)")
        }
    }
}
```

# Skill: writing-plans

# Writing Plans

## Overview

Write comprehensive implementation plans assuming the engineer has zero context for our codebase and questionable taste. Document everything they need to know: which files to touch for each task, code, testing, docs they might need to check, how to test it. Give them the whole plan as bite-sized tasks. DRY. YAGNI. TDD. Frequent commits.

Assume they are a skilled developer, but know almost nothing about our toolset or problem domain. Assume they don't know good test design very well.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the writing-plans skill to create the implementation plan."

**Context:** If working in an isolated worktree, it should have been created via the `superpowers:using-git-worktrees` skill at execution time.

**Save plans to:** `docs/superpowers/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<feature-name>.md`
- (User preferences for plan location override this default)

## Scope Check

If the spec covers multiple independent subsystems, it should have been broken into sub-project specs during brainstorming. If it wasn't, suggest breaking this into separate plans — one per subsystem. Each plan should produce working, testable software on its own.

## File Structure

Before defining tasks, map out which files will be created or modified and what each one is responsible for. This is where decomposition decisions get locked in.

- Design units with clear boundaries and well-defined interfaces. Each file should have one clear responsibility.
- You reason best about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. Prefer smaller, focused files over large ones that do too much.
- Files that change together should live together. Split by responsibility, not by technical layer.
- In existing codebases, follow established patterns. If the codebase uses large files, don't unilaterally restructure - but if a file you're modifying has grown unwieldy, including a split in the plan is reasonable.

This structure informs the task decomposition. Each task should produce self-contained changes that make sense independently.

## Task Right-Sizing

A task is the smallest unit that carries its own test cycle and is worth a
fresh reviewer's gate. When drawing task boundaries: fold setup,
configuration, scaffolding, and documentation steps into the task whose
deliverable needs them; split only where a reviewer could meaningfully
reject one task while approving its neighbor. Each task ends with an
independently testable deliverable.

## Bite-Sized Task Granularity

**Each step is one action (2-5 minutes):**
- "Write the failing test" - step
- "Run it to make sure it fails" - step
- "Implement the minimal code to make the test pass" - step
- "Run the tests and make sure they pass" - step
- "Commit" - step

## Plan Document Header

**Every plan MUST start with this header:**

```markdown
# [Feature Name] Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** [One sentence describing what this builds]

**Architecture:** [2-3 sentences about approach]

**Tech Stack:** [Key technologies/libraries]

**Spec:** [path to the spec/design doc this plan implements — the plan
argues from the spec, so the spec travels with it; executors read both]

## Global Constraints

[The spec's project-wide requirements — version floors, dependency limits,
naming and copy rules, platform requirements — one line each, with exact
values copied verbatim from the spec. Every task's requirements implicitly
include this section.]

## Review Focus

[The five input classes or failure modes the spec implies but no task's
tests exercise that are most likely to bite a person using this software
— one line each, naming the input or condition and the behavior a
reasonable person would expect, most likely first. The spec is a vision
document: it says what the software must do, not everything it will
meet, and its silence on an input is not permission for that input to
break the program. Write the list here, once, with the spec in front of
you. Then, for each line, add the test that pins it to the task that
owns the code, in that task's own step style.]

---
```

## Task Structure

````markdown
### Task N: [Component Name]

**Files:**
- Create: `exact/path/to/file.py`
- Modify: `exact/path/to/existing.py:123-145`
- Test: `tests/exact/path/to/test.py`

**Interfaces:**
- Consumes: [what this task uses from earlier tasks — exact signatures]
- Produces: [what later tasks rely on — exact function names, parameter
  and return types. A task's implementer sees only their own task; this
  block is how they learn the names and types neighboring tasks use.]

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing test**

```python
def test_specific_behavior():
    result = function(input)
    assert result == expected
```

- [ ] **Step 2: Run test to verify it fails**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: FAIL with "function not defined"

- [ ] **Step 3: Write minimal implementation**

```python
def function(input):
    return expected
```

- [ ] **Step 4: Run test to verify it passes**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: PASS

- [ ] **Step 5: Commit**

```bash
git add tests/path/test.py src/path/file.py
git commit -m "feat: add specific feature"
```
````

## No Placeholders

Every step must contain the actual content an engineer needs. These are **plan failures** — never write them:
- "TBD", "TODO", "implement later", "fill in details"
- "Add appropriate error handling" / "add validation" / "handle edge cases"
- "Write tests for the above" (without actual test code)
- "Similar to Task N" (repeat the code — the engineer may be reading tasks out of order)
- Steps that describe what to do without showing how (code blocks required for code steps)
- References to types, functions, or methods not defined in any task

## Self-Review

After writing the complete plan, look at the spec with fresh eyes and check the plan against it. This is a checklist you run yourself — not a subagent dispatch.

**1. Spec coverage:** Skim each section/requirement in the spec. Can you point to a task that implements it? List any gaps.

**2. Placeholder scan:** Search your plan for red flags — any of the patterns from the "No Placeholders" section above. Fix them.

**3. Type consistency:** Do the types, method signatures, and property names you used in later tasks match what you defined in earlier tasks? A function called `clearLayers()` in Task 3 but `clearFullLayers()` in Task 7 is a bug.

**4. Review Focus:** For each input class or failure mode the spec implies, is there a task whose tests exercise it? The five uncovered ones most likely to bite a person go in the Review Focus section, and each line there gets its test added to the owning task. An empty section means you checked and found none, not that you skipped the check.

If you find issues, fix them inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on. If you find a spec requirement with no task, add the task.

## Execution Handoff

After saving and self-reviewing the plan, link it for your human partner
to read. If they have already explicitly supplied an execution method, ask
them to review the plan and confirm it captures what they want; wait for that
review before implementation, then use the preserved method. Otherwise, ask
them to review the plan and choose an execution method before implementation.

**When no execution method has already been supplied:**

**"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Please review the plan. Which execution approach would you prefer?**

- **Subagent-driven** - A fresh subagent implements each task and a fresh reviewer checks it before the next one starts, then a whole-branch review at the end. Most thorough; costs a fresh context per task and per review.
- **Native** - I implement every task myself in this session, the way this harness runs work, then one fresh reviewer on the most capable model checks the whole branch. Cheapest and fastest; no independent review until the end. Runs well with a mid-tier session model, since the plan carries the design.

**For this plan I recommend <one of the two>, because <one sentence from the plan: how much the tasks depend on each other's interfaces, how many there are, what a shipped mistake would cost>. Does the plan capture what you want, and which approach should we use?"**

**When an execution method has already been supplied:**

**"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Please review the plan. Does it capture what you want?"**

**If Subagent-driven chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development

**If Native chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:executing-plans

# Tether — spécification de conception

**Date** : 2026-09-24
**Statut** : validé par Bastien (sections 1 à 8), en attente de revue du spec écrit
**Auteur** : session opencode le serveur

---

## 1. Contexte & objectif

Bastien pilote opencode **v2.0.x** sur le serveur (192.0.2.10) depuis son poste de
travail. Il veut **retrouver et piloter ses sessions depuis son téléphone**, sans
dépendre du rendu mobile — qu'il juge mauvais — de l'interface web d'opencode.

**Tether est le contrôleur mobile d'opencode.** Toutes les sessions de le serveur dans
la poche, visibles et pilotables **en direct, dans les deux sens**.

### Le problème réel

Un serveur opencode LAN existe déjà (`opencode-remote.service`, `0.0.0.0:4096`, active
depuis le 23/09) et sert depuis le rebuild du 23/09 l'UI web V2 complète. Mais :

- **Trois serveurs concurrents** sur la même base : le service de fond
  (`127.0.0.1:4097`), le serveur LAN (`:4096`), et les sessions TUI. Les sessions sont
  communes, mais **aucun direct n'est partagé** : ce qui est tapé au clavier n'apparaît
  pas en flux sur le téléphone.
- **L'UI web est inutilisable sur Android** : rendu dense non adapté, pas d'app
  installable, pas de notifications, pas d'accès hors LAN.
- **Aucun client Android natif opencode V2 n'existe** (vérifié sur pièces, cf. §16).
  Les clients Kotlin populaires (`starburst`, `oc-remote`, `P4OC`) sont tous **V1**.
- **Aucun client opencode n'implémente UnifiedPush.**

### Objectif mesurable

Depuis le Pixel 9 Pro Fold (GrapheneOS), pouvoir : voir la liste des sessions de
le serveur, ouvrir une session, écrire au clavier **ou à la voix**, suivre la réponse en
streaming, et **répondre aux demandes d'approbation de l'agent**. Sur notification
d'attention, un tap rouvre **la bonne session** pour valider ou interdire.

---

## 2. Périmètre

### Dans le périmètre

- Application **Android native Kotlin / Jetpack Compose** (jamais une PWA).
- Client de l'API opencode **V2** (`/api/*`), transport SSE + REST.
- Interface de chat moderne (façon ChatGPT / Gemini) : streaming, markdown, cartes
  d'outils, diffs, rapports de sous-agents.
- **Bidirectionnel** : approbations d'outils (`once` / `always` / `reject`) et
  **formulaires structurés** répondus depuis le téléphone.
- **Dictée vocale** vers le whisper self-hosted (TrueNAS `:8300`).
- **Notifications** UnifiedPush (via ntfy self-hosted) : session finie / en attente /
  en échec, avec deep link vers la session.
- Notification de **nouvelle version** de l'app.
- Accès **hors LAN** via `tether.example.com` derrière Pocket-ID.

### Hors périmètre (assumé)

- Terminal PTY, panneau Git, widgets d'écran d'accueil, base de connaissances.
- Orchestration multi-agents (Claude Code, Codex…). **opencode uniquement.**
- Mode conversationnel vocal : **pas de wake word, pas de TTS, pas de VAD**. Dictée
  seule.
- Application grand public. Un utilisateur, un homelab.

---

## 3. Décisions validées

| # | Décision | Statut |
|---|---|---|
| D1 | **Nom : Tether** (référence à `opencode` « attach ») | ✅ validé |
| D2 | **Mono-serveur** : le TUI du PC devient client du serveur LAN | ✅ validé |
| D3 | **App Android native Kotlin/Compose**, jamais PWA | ✅ validé |
| D4 | **Hors-LAN derrière Pocket-ID** (jamais de basic auth exposé) | ✅ validé |
| D5 | **Approbations depuis le téléphone**, notif cliquable → bonne session | ✅ validé |
| D6 | **UnifiedPush** sur fin de session / attente / échec | ✅ validé |
| D7 | **Dictée seule** (pas de mode conversationnel complet) | ✅ validé |
| D8 | **From-scratch**, pas de fork (cf. §15) | ✅ validé |

### Design system validé

- Dark-first, dense, calme. Pas de néon décoratif.
- Fonds `#0B0E11` / surfaces `#11151A` ; texte `#E6EDF3`, secondaire `#8B98A5`.
- Accent actif / streaming : **teal `#2DD4BF`**. Accent d'alerte (approbation, erreur) :
  **ambre `#FFB020`**, réservé.
- Typographie : **Inter** (UI) + **JetBrains Mono** (code, chemins, diffs).
- Logo : **deux nœuds reliés par une corde légèrement tendue** (le « tether ») ; nœud
  téléphone plein, nœud PC en anneau. Adaptive icon Android, vectoriel, lisible à 48 px.

---

## 4. Architecture

### 4.1 Mono-serveur (D2)

```
                    ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
   PC (TUI) ────────►  opencode --server http://127.0.0.1:4096 │
                    │                                          │
   Pixel (Tether) ──►  opencode-remote.service  :4096          │
                    │  (0.0.0.0, basic auth)                   │
   [hors LAN] ──────►  tether.example.com → SWAG → Pocket-ID ───────┤
                    └──────────────────────────────────────────┘
                                    │
                            opencode.db (une seule base)
```

- `opencode-remote.service` (`/usr/local/bin/opencode serve --hostname 0.0.0.0 --port 4096`)
  reste **LE** serveur.
- Le TUI du poste se connecte avec **`opencode --server <url>`** (le flag `--server`
  remplace `attach` en V2 — ⚠️ `attach` **n'existe plus**, vérifié sur le binaire 2.0.x).
- **Prérequis** : neutraliser le **service de fond** (`127.0.0.1:4097`), sinon un
  `opencode` lancé sans flag repart sur un deuxième serveur. Il n'existe **aucune clé de
  configuration persistante** pour la connexion client (`opencode service get` ne
  connaît que `{hostname, port}` du service de fond) → alias shell + désactivation du
  service de fond.
- **Conséquence assumée** : le terminal du PC passe par le réseau local au lieu du
  socket local. Négligeable en LAN filaire.

### 4.2 Transport

- **REST `/api/*`** pour tout l'état : sessions, messages, modèles, agents, projets,
  permissions en attente, formulaires.
- **SSE `GET /api/event`** pour le direct : `Last-Event-ID`, reconnexion automatique.
- ⚠️ **Filtrage `content-type` obligatoire** : sur un serveur V2, les anciennes routes
  V1 renvoient `200 text/html` = fallback SPA, **pas** une route. Un client SSE qui
  reçoit un `Content-Type` non `text/event-stream` cesse de retenter (piège KTOR-9023).
- **Règle d'or — la vérité vient du REST, jamais du flux.** Resync complet de la session
  à chaque reconnexion ; le SSE sert à l'instantané, pas à la correction.
- **L'API V2 est *location-scoped*** : `?location[directory]=<absolu>` en query, ou
  `location: {directory}` dans le corps de `POST /api/session`. Sans répertoire,
  `/api/agent` renvoie `data: []` **sans erreur**.

### 4.3 Flux d'un prompt (le point qui change tout)

1. `POST /api/session/{sid}/prompt` avec `{text, files?, model?, delivery?}`.
   ⚠️ Le corps porte **`text`**, pas `{model, parts}` (ancien V2 du 23/09).
2. La réponse **n'est pas un message** mais un **item d'inbox** (`msg_*` →
   `SessionInboxInfo`), livré ensuite par l'événement `session.inbox.delivered`.
3. Le contenu de l'assistant arrive **par le flux**, sous forme de **`content[]` typé et
   encodé** dans `session.message.content.updated` — **plus de modèle « message + parts »**.
4. Le modèle se fixe **à la création de la session** (`POST /api/session` avec
   `model: {id, providerID}`), ou se change ensuite par
   `POST /api/session/{sid}/model`.

---

## 5. Référence API V2 — le contrat

Contrat reconstitué depuis le seul client V2 réel (`omnicus/opencode2-mobile`,
`packages/opencode-adapter/src/index.ts`, MIT) et le client officiel
`@opencode/client@2.0.16` (`types.d.ts`). **À re-valider par test live** contre le
serveur de Bastien (§15).

### 5.1 Endpoints

| Besoin | Route |
|---|---|
| Info serveur | `GET /api/info` |
| Location / projets | `GET /api/location`, `GET /api/project` |
| Modèles / agents / commandes | `GET /api/model`, `GET /api/agent`, `GET /api/command` |
| Sessions | `GET /api/session`, `POST /api/session`, `GET /api/session/{sid}`, `DELETE /api/session/{sid}` |
| Messages | `GET /api/session/{sid}/message`, `GET /api/session/{sid}/message/{mid}` |
| Prompt | `POST /api/session/{sid}/prompt` |
| Interrompre | `POST /api/session/{sid}/interrupt` |
| Modèle / agent d'une session | `POST /api/session/{sid}/model`, `POST /api/session/{sid}/agent` |
| Événements (SSE) | `GET /api/event` |
| **Permissions en attente** | `GET /api/permission/request` |
| **Répondre à une permission** | `POST /api/session/{sid}/permission/{rid}/reply` |
| **Formulaires en attente** | `GET /api/form`, `GET /api/session/{sid}/form/{fid}` |
| **Répondre à un formulaire** | `POST /api/session/{sid}/form/{fid}/reply` |
| Annuler un formulaire | `DELETE /api/session/{sid}/form/{fid}` |

Enveloppes : les listes renvoient `{data: [...], cursor: {previous?, next?}}`.
`/api/location` renvoie `{directory, project:{id,directory,canonical}, workspaceID?}`.

### 5.2 DTOs clés

```ts
PermissionRequest    = { id, sessionID, action, resources: string[], save?: string[],
                         metadata?, source?, message? }
PermissionReplyInput = { sessionID, requestID, decision: "once"|"always"|"reject", message? }
SessionFormReplyInput= { sessionID, formID, answer: { [champ]: string|number|boolean|string[] } }
SessionPromptInput   = { sessionID, id? (/^msg_/), text, files?: {uri,name?,description?}[],
                         agents?, skills?, delivery?: "steer"|"queue", model? }
```

`decision: "always"` = approuve **et mémorise les motifs proposés pour le projet**
(durable, projet-scoped, ne peut jamais casser un `deny` configuré).
`decision: "reject"` = refuse **et rejette toutes les autres demandes pendantes de la
session**.

### 5.3 Événements SSE utiles

| Domaine | Événements |
|---|---|
| Serveur | `server.connected` |
| **Attention (notifs)** | **`permission.asked`**, **`permission.replied`**, **`form.created`**, **`form.replied`**, **`form.cancelled`** |
| Exécution (notifs) | **`session.execution.started` / `.succeeded` / `.failed` / `.interrupted`** |
| Texte | `session.text.started` / `.delta` / `.ended` |
| Raisonnement | `session.reasoning.started` / `.delta` / `.ended` |
| Outils | `session.tool.input.started` / `.delta` / `.ended`, `session.tool.called` / `.progress` / `.success` / `.failed` |
| Contenu | **`session.message.content.updated`** (remplace `message.part.updated` V1) |
| Étapes | `session.step.started` / `.ended` / `.failed` / `.streamed` |
| Inbox | `session.inbox.enqueued` / `.delivered` / `.cancelled` / `.delivery.changed` |
| Sessions | `session.created` / `.updated` / `.deleted` / `.forked` / `.moved` / `.renamed` / `.status` / `.idle` |
| Divers | `session.usage.recorded` / `.updated`, `session.compaction.ended` / `.failed`, `session.retry.scheduled`, `session.synthetic` |

⚠️ **Forme d'enveloppe V2** : `{id, created, type, durable, location, data}`. Le
`sessionID` est dans **`data.sessionID`** — ni à la racine, ni dans `properties` (formes
V1). Leçon tirée du portage du plugin `ntfy-opencode` (§7).

---

## 6. Composants de l'application

Application monomodule ou peu modulaire, Kotlin + Compose, Hilt, Ktor client,
kotlinx-serialization. **Aucune dépendance Play Services / Firebase / GMS.**

| Composant | Rôle |
|---|---|
| `data/api` | Client REST V2 typé (Ktor), DTOs, enveloppes `{data,cursor}`, gestion `location` |
| `data/event` | Client SSE `/api/event`, parseur d'événements V2, reconnexion + `Last-Event-ID`, **filtrage content-type** |
| `data/repository` | `EventReducer` (réduit le flux en état de session), `SessionRepository`, `PermissionRepository`, `FormRepository`, persistance locale (drafts) |
| `domain/model` | `Session`, `Message`, `AssistantContent` (typé), `ToolCall`, `PermissionRequest`, `Form` |
| `ui/chat` | Écran de conversation : streaming, markdown GFM, blocs de code, coloration, bouton copier, **cartes d'outils dépliables**, diffs unifiés, sous-agents imbriqués |
| `ui/approval` | **Carte bloquante** d'approbation (plein écran) et formulaire structuré |
| `ui/sessions` | Drawer projet → session, état, coût/tokens, modèle/agent, bouton stop |
| `ui/settings` | Connexion serveur, Pocket-ID, thème, serveur STT, à propos/MAJ |
| `ml/dictation` | Enregistreur audio + client whisper |
| `service/connection` | Foreground service : maintien du SSE en arrière-plan |
| `push` | Client UnifiedPush (connector), receiver, service `RAISE_TO_FOREGROUND` |
| `update` | Vérification de version (Gitea), installation APK |

Bibliothèques prévues (validées par la recon) : Compose BOM, **Ktor 2.3+** (okhttp engine,
SSE), **Hilt**, **kotlinx-serialization**, `mikepenz/multiplatform-markdown-renderer`,
**Coil**, `com.composables:icons-lucide` (léger, préféré à material-icons-extended).
`minSdk 26`, cible à confirmer (34 ou 35). **Pas de Gson** (doublon inutile).

---

## 7. Notifications

Deux canaux **distincts**.

### 7.1 UnifiedPush — état des sessions (D6)

```
opencode /api/event ──► plugin V2 serveur ──► endpoint UP (Web Push chiffré) ──► ntfy-android ──► Tether
```

- **Côté serveur : un plugin opencode V2.** ⚠️ **Le plugin maison `ntfy-opencode`
  existe déjà** (`~/.config/opencode/plugins/ntfy-opencode.ts`, porté V2 le 20/09) et
  couvre déjà : souscription aux événements, détection de fin de tour
  (`session.execution.succeeded/.failed/.interrupted`), extraction du dernier message
  assistant, résumé par le LLM local (ornith_router `:8099`), publication ntfy.
  **Ce qui manque** :
  1. écouter **`permission.asked`** et **`form.created`** → notif « L'agent de Tether
     requiert votre attention » ;
  2. publier vers les **endpoints UP par appareil** (Web Push chiffré, RFC 8291) au lieu
     du seul topic `OpenCode` ;
  3. joindre une **deep link** (`opencode://session/<sid>`) pour rouvrir la bonne session.
- **Côté téléphone** : Tether s'enregistre comme application UnifiedPush auprès de
  **ntfy-android** (distributeur UP officiel, Apache/GPL).
  - Bibliothèque : `org.unifiedpush.android` (via JitPack — coordonnée exacte à
    confirmer, §15).
  - Obligatoire : un `MessagingBroadcastReceiver` (`NEW_ENDPOINT`, `MESSAGE`,
    `UNREGISTERED`, `REGISTRATION_FAILED`, `TEMP_UNAVAILABLE`) **et** un service
    `RAISE_TO_FOREGROUND`.
  - L'endpoint reçu (`https://ntfy.example.com/upXXXX`) est transmis au serveur d'application
    (le plugin opencode) — c'est lui qui publie dessus.
- **Contraintes ntfy self-hosted** :
  - Les topics UnifiedPush commencent par **`up*`** → l'ACL doit les rendre
    **write-only en anonyme** : `ntfy access '*' 'up*' write-only`.
  - L'endpoint doit être **joignable depuis le serveur d'application** (LAN
    `192.0.2.20:7171` ou public `ntfy.example.com`).
- **GrapheneOS** : pas de Play Services → le fallback FCM embarqué est inopérant :
  **ntfy-android est la seule voie propre**. ntfy doit être **exempté d'optimisation
  batterie**.
- Limites connues : un enregistrement sans `MESSAGE_ACK` depuis 30 jours est
  désenregistré ; le distributeur doit élever l'app en importance 5 s par message.

### 7.2 ntfy direct — nouvelle version

Publication simple sur un **topic dédié** (séparé de l'UP) : « Tether vX.Y dispo » +
lien. Aucun rapport avec UnifiedPush.

---

## 8. Dictée vocale (D7)

Appui long sur le micro → enregistrement → relâchement → envoi à **whisper self-hosted**
(TrueNAS `:8300`, RTX 4060). La transcription **atterrit dans le champ de saisie,
éditable, jamais envoyée automatiquement** — indispensable pour un prompt technique
contenant des chemins et des identifiants.

- LAN : `192.0.2.20:8300`. Hors-LAN : `whisper.example.com` (proxy déjà en place, auth 401).
- Réseau absent → le bouton se désactive au lieu d'échouer.
- **Aucun** wake word, **aucun** TTS, **aucun** mode conversationnel.

---

## 9. Sécurité

Trois règles, justifiées par le fait que l'agent a `bash` sur le serveur.

**S1 — Une notification forgée ne peut rien approuver.**
C'est structurel : l'ACL UnifiedPush impose les topics `up*` en écriture anonyme, donc
n'importe qui connaissant le topic peut publier. Mais **la notification ne porte aucune
capacité** : le tap ouvre l'app, et **l'app relit l'état réel** (`GET /api/permission/request`)
avant d'afficher. Une fausse notif peut au pire ouvrir une session vide ; elle ne peut
jamais faire approuver un `rm`. Le plugin serveur ne publie qu'un **type d'événement
catégorisé** (allowlist finie), **jamais de payload brut** — modèle repris du broker
d'`opencode2-mobile`.

**S2 — « Toujours autoriser » exige la biométrie.**
`always` **persiste pour le projet** : c'est le seul choix irréversible des trois.
`once` et `reject` tiennent en un tap. **Jamais d'approbation à la voix** : la dictée
sert à écrire des prompts, pas à signer.

**S3 — Signalement explicite du danger.**
L'action demandée est affichée **brute et en clair** (commande, chemins), marquée ambre
quand elle touche `shell` avec des motifs destructeurs (`rm`, `dd`, `mkfs`, `sudo`,
`chown`, redirection vers un chemin système). **On signale, on ne prétend pas bloquer** :
le garde-fou réel est l'œil de l'utilisateur, l'app lui donne tout.

**S4 — Hors-LAN : Pocket-ID.** `tether.example.com` via SWAG → OIDC (PKCE + Custom Tabs).
opencode ne sait faire que du basic auth → il faut un **proxy d'authentification** devant
lui. **Composant à concevoir**, pas un flag (cf. §10).

---

## 10. Accès hors-LAN

`tether.example.com` → SWAG (VPS IncogNET `23.137.251.136`) → **Pocket-ID**
(`auth.example.com`) → opencode `:4096`.

Point ouvert : le mécanisme exact du proxy d'authentification (une passerelle qui valide
le JWT Pocket-ID puis relaie avec le basic auth opencode). À spécifier en phase 4 ;
options : petit reverse-proxy dédié (Node/Go) avec validation OIDC, ou `oauth2-proxy`
devant un vhost SWAG. **À trancher au moment de la phase 4**, pas avant.

---

## 11. UI & identité

### Écran de chat (le cœur)

- Message utilisateur compact à droite ; réponse assistant pleine largeur.
- **Streaming token par token** (`session.text.delta`).
- **Markdown complet** : listes, tables, code avec coloration et bouton copier.
- **Cartes d'outils dépliables** : nom, arguments, sortie, statut. Repliées par défaut,
  **les erreurs s'ouvrent seules**.
- **Rapports de sous-agents imbriqués** (jamais jetés).
- **Diffs** en vue unifiée, fonds vert/rouge.

### Approbation

**Carte bloquante plein écran** — pas un toast : l'outil, l'action exacte, les ressources,
et trois boutons `Autoriser une fois` / `Toujours autoriser` (biométrie) / `Refuser`.
Les **formulaires** V2 (multi-champs typés) ont leur propre écran.

### Navigation

Drawer/rail → projet → session. En tête de session : modèle et agent changeables, coût et
tokens, statut. Bouton stop (`POST /api/session/{sid}/interrupt`). Bouton `+` pour créer
une session **en choisissant le modèle dès le départ** (contrainte API).

### Identité

Palette, typo et logo définis en §3. Le logo et l'adaptive icon sont produits au moment
du scaffold et **présentés en image avant d'être figés**.

---

## 12. Distribution & mise à jour

- **Gitea releases** (`git.example.com`) pour les APK signés, dépôt `utilisateur/tether`.
- **Updater in-app** (`REQUEST_INSTALL_PACKAGES`, vérification de signature) — décision
  motivée : **Obtainium ne supporte pas Gitea nativement** (Forgejo oui ; Gitea seulement
  des issues ouvertes #2606 / #3167, contournement par source « HTML » non testé). Pas de
  dépendance à un contournement.
- Notif « nouvelle version dispo » sur le topic ntfy dédié (§7.2).
- **Licence** : point ouvert (cf. §15).

---

## 13. Stratégie de vérification

Le vrai risque est le **parsing du flux et la réduction d'état**, pas l'UI.

1. **Tests unitaires** : parseur SSE V2, `EventReducer`, rendu des `content[]` typés,
   réponse aux permissions/formulaires. Inspirés du MIT d'`oc-remote`
   (`EventReducerTest.kt`, `PendingInteraction.kt`) — inspiration, pas copie.
2. **Tests d'intégration** contre le **serveur V2 réel** de le serveur, en réutilisant
   la fixture mock d'`opencode2-mobile` (`packages/test-fixtures`, MIT) comme oracle.
3. **E2E sur le Pixel** via ADB : créer une session, envoyer un prompt, recevoir un
   stream, approuver un outil depuis le téléphone, vérifier la notif UP.
4. **Vérification par `verify`** avant chaque jalon.

---

## 14. Phasage

| Phase | Contenu | Critère de sortie |
|---|---|---|
| **0 — Infra** | Mono-serveur (alias `oc` + neutraliser le service de fond), chaîne de build Android (SDK cmdline-tools + **JDK 21** — le poste a un Java 26 trop récent et aucun SDK installé), extension du plugin `ntfy-opencode` (permissions/forms + endpoints UP), topics ntfy + ACL `up*` | `opencode --server` fonctionne ; `curl` SSE renvoie du `text/event-stream` ; une notif UP arrive sur le Pixel |
| **1 — MVP chat** | Couche data V2, connexion, liste des sessions, chat streaming markdown, envoi de prompt, création de session avec modèle | Écrire et lire une session depuis le téléphone |
| **2 — Bidirectionnel** | Approbations (`once`/`always` biométrie/`reject`), formulaires, notif UP + deep link vers la bonne session, foreground service | Approuver une commande `shell` depuis le téléphone |
| **3 — Dictée** | Enregistreur + client whisper TrueNAS | Dicter un prompt, le corriger, l'envoyer |
| **4 — Extérieur & confort** | `tether.example.com` + Pocket-ID, updater in-app, logo final, E2E complet | Utilisable en 4G depuis l'extérieur |

---

## 15. Risques & points ouverts

### Décisions non tranchées

1. **Licence du projet** — « application open source » vs privée n'est pas explicitement
   tranché dans la formulation initiale. Recommandation : **GPL-3.0** (cohérent avec
   l'esprit de `oc-remote`) ou **MIT**. À confirmer avant le premier commit public.
2. **Proxy d'authentification Pocket-ID** (§10) : mécanisme exact à choisir en phase 4.
3. **Mono-serveur** : méthode de neutralisation du service de fond (§4.1) — à valider en
   phase 0 sans casser les sessions en cours.
4. **Coordonnée Maven** exacte du connector UnifiedPush (JitPack) — à confirmer.
5. **`targetSdk`** : 34 ou 35.

### Risques techniques

| Risque | Gravité | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| Le contrat API V2 est reconstitué, **pas confirmé live** (les DTOs viennent d'un client tiers) | **élevée** | Valider chaque endpoint contre le serveur réel dès la phase 0/1 ; la fixture mock sert d'oracle |
| Le prompt V2 renvoie un **item d'inbox**, pas un message → l'UI doit être pensée « inbox » | moyenne | Intégré au design (§4.3) |
| Contenu assistant = **`content[]` typé et encodé**, plus « message + parts » | moyenne | Modèle de domaine dédié (§6) |
| Publication **Web Push chiffré** vers l'endpoint UP (RFC 8291) côté plugin | moyenne | À vérifier contre la doc ntfy ; repli : publier sur le topic `up*` si ntfy l'accepte en clair |
| **SSE en arrière-plan** tué par Doze | moyenne | Foreground service + **resync REST** à la reconnexion |
| Ambiguïté MIT / « All rights reserved » des repos pillés | faible | On ne prend **ni code ni binaire** : seulement des idées d'architecture |

### Ce qui n'a pas pu être confirmé par la recon

- Disparition effective de l'API V1 sur l'instance 2.0.x (jamais testée live).
- Support natif Gitea d'Obtainium (contournement par source « HTML » non testé).
- Timeout serveur d'une demande de permission non répondue.
- Coordonnée Maven du connector UnifiedPush.
- TTS dans `starburst` (non pertinent — hors périmètre).
- Absence de build/run réel (pas d'Android SDK sur le poste à ce stade).

---

## 16. Pourquoi from-scratch (annexe — décision D8)

Inspection sur pièces de trois clients (clones read-only, chiffres mesurés) :

| | starburst | oc-remote | from-scratch |
|---|---|---|---|
| Kotlin | 82 000 LOC, 315 fichiers, 33 écrans | 39 000 LOC | 0 |
| Couche API V2 | **0 %** (V1 ; 3 stubs V2 jamais branchés) | **0 %** (V1, stale 18 j) | à écrire |
| APK | 27,8 Mo (dont ~20 Mo de `.so` MNN opaques) | 5,3 Mo | ~6-8 Mo |
| Licence | MIT **mais** headers `Copyright Clouds Studio — All rights reserved` par fichier ; backend Go **sans LICENSE** | MIT propre | au choix |
| Portage estimé | **15-25 j-h** | idem | ~20-30 j-h |

**Décision : from-scratch.** Le travail incompressible est identique — **aucun** des trois
n'a de couche V2, donc dans tous les cas il faut écrire le client REST `/api/*`, le parseur
SSE et le réducteur d'événements. Ce que le fork économiserait, c'est une UI que Bastien
ne veut pas, couplée aux vieux DTO V1 (≈ 22 000 LOC de call sites à traverser), et le seul
composant différenciant de `starburst` (STT on-device MNN) est **inutile** puisque la
dictée passe par whisper TrueNAS — son `ServerAsrApi` ne tape d'ailleurs pas sur whisper
mais sur son backend Go, sans licence.

**Ce qu'on pille — idées et docs uniquement, aucun code, aucun binaire :**

- `omnicus/opencode2-mobile` (MIT) — **le seul client V2 réel** : `packages/opencode-adapter/src/index.ts`
  (1 899 LOC), les DTOs et la liste d'endpoints ; `packages/test-fixtures` comme oracle de test.
- `@opencode/client@2.0.16` — `types.d.ts`, spec officielle des types.
- `crim50n/oc-remote` (MIT) — inspiration d'architecture : `EventReducer.kt`,
  `domain/model/PendingInteraction.kt` (le modèle le plus clair des trois).
- Le broker d'`opencode2-mobile` — **modèle de sécurité** : allowlist de types
  d'événements, jamais de payload brut.

---

## 17. Fichiers de référence

| Ressource | Chemin |
|---|---|
| Plugin ntfy existant (à étendre) | `~/.config/opencode/plugins/ntfy-opencode.ts` |
| Serveur LAN | `~/.config/systemd/user/opencode-remote.service` |
| Secrets serveur | `~/.config/opencode/ocremote-{password,env}` |
| Pont OWUI (contexte) | `~/Projects/opencode-bridge/` |
| Recon sur pièces (clones) | `/tmp/opencode/recon-tether/` |
| Spec officielle opencode V2 | `https://opencode.ai/v2/openapi.json` |

Clones dans `/tmp/opencode/recon-tether/`. Aucune modif, aucun push. Date d'inspection : 24/09/2026. HEAD git de chaque repo relevé ci-dessous.

---

## 1. `hiylo/starburst` — candidat principal

### Taille / structure (chiffres mesurés)

| Métrique | Valeur |
|---|---|
| HEAD | `e155c6b` — 2026-09-23 (actif, 2 j avant inspect) |
| Fichiers `.kt` | **315** |
| Lignes Kotlin `src/main` | **82 038** |
| Lignes Kotlin `src/test` + `androidTest` | 5 372 (**70 fichiers** de test) |
| Taille repo | 39 Mo dont **~20 Mo de `jniLibs`** (MNN/sherpa précompilés arm64+v7a) |
| Écrans Compose (`*Screen.kt`) | 33 |
| ViewModels | 39 |
| `@Composable` (total, 84 fichiers) | **388** |
| APK release v3.0.0 | **27,78 Mo** (`app-release-v3.0.0.apk`) |
| Stars / forks / issues | 6 / 0 / 7 ouverts — projet très jeune |

Modules Gradle : `:app` + `:baselineprofile` (`settings.gradle.kts`). `minSdk=26`, `targetSdk=34`, `compileSdk=34`, AGP **8.4.0**, Kotlin **2.0.21**, Gradle 8.6, Java 17, `ndkVersion 27.2.12479018` + CMake 3.22.1.

Structure applicative (`app/src/main/kotlin/org/hiylo/starburst/`) : `data/{api,backend,backup,repository,search,shell,sync,update}`, `domain/model`, `ml`, `service`, `ui/{components,navigation,screens/*,theme}`, `widget`.

Couches clés en LOC :
- `data/api/` : **4 939 LOC** (21 fichiers)
- `domain/model/` : **1 420 LOC** (dont `Part.kt` 267, `Message.kt` 154, `SseEvent.kt` 388)
- `data/repository/` : 5 463 LOC
- `ui/screens/chat/` : **22 724 LOC** (15 fichiers, dont `ChatInputBar.kt` 1 306, `TerminalEmulator.kt` 1 278)

### ⚠️ La couche API est **100 % V1** — c'est le point qui change tout

Malgré le nom de version « 3.0.0 », l'app parle la **surface V1 d'opencode**, pas `/api/*` V2. Preuve (`OpenCodeApi.kt` / `SseClient.kt` / `OpenCodeApiMessages.kt`) :

```
${conn.baseUrl}/global/event        <- SSE V1, pas GET /api/event
${conn.baseUrl}/session             <- liste V1
${conn.baseUrl}/session/$sessionId/prompt_async
${conn.baseUrl}/permission/$requestId/reply   (body: {reply:"once"|"always"|"reject"})
${conn.baseUrl}/permission                     (liste V1)
${conn.baseUrl}/question/$requestId/reply      (body {answers:[][]})
${conn.baseUrl}/question/$requestId/reject
${conn.baseUrl}/pty, /file, /find, /config/providers, /mcp/{name}/auth...
```

Les **seuls** appels V2 présents sont **morts** :
- `promptV2()` → `POST /api/session/{sid}/prompt` (`OpenCodeApiMessages.kt:182`)
- `switchSessionAgentV2()` → `POST /api/session/{sid}/agent` (`OpenCodeApiMeta.kt:413`)
- `switchSessionModelV2()` → `POST /api/session/{sid}/model` (`OpenCodeApiMeta.kt:430`)

J'ai cherché leurs call sites : **0 pour les trois**. Ce sont des stubs écrits puis jamais branchés. Le flux réel passe par `prompt_async` (V1).

Le parseur SSE (`SseClient.kt:80` lit `/global/event`) ne connaît que les **noms V1** `session.next.text.delta`, `session.next.tool.called`, `message.part.updated`, `session.next.step.*`, `permission.asked`… `SseEvent.kt` compte **61 data classes**. Aucun des noms V2 (`session.text.delta`, `session.tool.called`, `session.step.*`, `session.execution.succeeded`, `session.inbox.*`).

Conclusion : **starburst v3.0.0 ne peut pas piloter opencode 2.0.x**. Soit l'API V1 a disparu, soit elle est legacy. L'app doit être portée sur `/api/*` pour fonctionner chez Bastien.

### Réutilisable tel quel

Tout ce qui est **UI/média/device**, indépendant du transport :

- **Chat Compose** : markdown GFM, code blocks, syntax highlighting, streaming, auto-scroll, cartes d'outils dépliables, diff, images (Coil), 388 composables. (`ui/screens/chat/*`)
- **STT on-device** — `ml/MnnAsr.kt` (336), `ml/MnnAsrRecorder.kt` (169), `ml/AsrSession.kt` (51) via MNN sherpa streaming Zipformer, modèles téléchargés ModelScope avec SHA-256.
- **STT serveur** — `ml/ServerAsrApi.kt` (169) + `ml/ServerAsrRecorder.kt` (225) : `POST /api/stt/sessions`, chunks, finish, refine.
- **TTS** : je n'ai pas trouvé de module TTS dédié dans `ml/` (MnnLlm.kt est un LLM de suggestions). **À confirmer**.
- **PTY/WebSocket** : `PtySocket` (`OpenCodeApi.kt:352`), `ChatTerminal.kt`, `TerminalEmulator.kt` (1 278 LOC) — mais branché sur `/pty` **V1**.
- **Git** : `ui/screens/git/` — mais opère via PTY/shell + `/session/{id}/diff` V1.
- **Widget** : `widget/` (4 fichiers, snapshot d'état).
- **Multi-serveurs** : `ServerConfig.kt`, `ServerConnection`, service de connexion par serveur.
- **Permissions/questions (UI)** : `PendingInteraction.kt`, `ChatOverlayCards.kt`, cartes `permission.asked`/`question.asked` — la **logique est bonne, les endpoints sont V1**.
- **Notifications** : locales uniquement (`SessionNotificationCoordinator.kt`, `NotificationReplyReceiver.kt`, foreground service). **Aucun FCM/GMS** → compatible GrapheneOS.
- **Persistent PTY**, SSH (JSch), sync multi-device, bookmarks, recherche full-text, thèmes.

### Le backend Go `hiylo/starburst-backend`

- Go 1.25, **98 routes HTTP**, dont 56 sous `/api/intel/*`. C'est un orchestrateur lourd : tasks, batch, archives, événements cron/webhook, KB vectorielle, génération de docs, LLM proxy, **test intelligence**.
- Dépendances côté app : `data/api/BackendApi.kt` (853 LOC), `BackendKbApi`, `BackendDocumentsApi`, `BackendSync`, `BackendAlerts`, `IntelModels` (285), `data/backend/*` → **~2 500 LOC** d'appels réseau vers le backend, plus `ui/screens/{kb,tasks,workbench,server,testintel}`.
- **Réponse à la question clé** : le backend est **optionnel pour le chat**. `OpenCodeGateway.kt` implémente un fallback : si le backend n'est pas joignable, l'app parle **directement** à opencode (`OpenCodeGateway.resolve()` retourne la connexion brute). Le chat, le terminal, git, fichiers fonctionnent sans backend. Le backend n'apporte que l'orchestration/intel/KB/push.
- **Verdict** : on peut l'éliminer entièrement en parlant direct à V2. Il faudra juste supprimer/parker les écrans `kb`, `tasks`, `workbench`, `testintel` et les `Backend*Api`.
- **⚠️ Pas de LICENSE dans `starburst-backend`** (aucun fichier `LICENSE`/`COPYING`). Repo sans licence = tous droits réservés par défaut. Ne pas redistribuer ce binaire.
- **⚠️ Point juridique starburst app** : le repo est MIT, mais **chaque fichier porte un en-tête `Copyright(c) 2016 - Present, Clouds Studio Holding Limited. All rights reserved.`** (ex. `OpenCodeApi.kt:1-9`). Un MIT à la racine + headers « All rights reserved » par fichier = ambiguïté à trancher avant redistribution commerciale. À signaler comme risque, pas comme blocage certain.

### Qualité

- Tests : 70 fichiers, 5 372 LOC (`src/test` + `src/androidTest`), dont tests de parseur SSE et réducteur.
- CI : `.github/workflows/{ci,release,secret-scan}.yml`. E2E Maestro (`e2e/*.yml`).
- Dépendances **lourdes** : MNN + sherpa précompilés (20 Mo de `.so`), `com.github.mwiede:jsch:0.2.20`, `androidx.webkit` (fallback legacy), `com.google.code.gson` en plus de kotlinx-serialization. Aucune Play Services/Firebase/GMS détectée.
- `kapt` (pas KSP), Hilt 2.52.

### Part du produit cible déjà là

Surface **UI/device** : ~70-75 % (chat, markdown, outils, diff, images, git, terminal, STT on-device **et** serveur, widget, multi-serveurs, notifications locales).
Surface **transport V2** : **~0 %**. Permissions/forms V2 : **0 %** (logique V1 réutilisable).
Le chat lui-même ne fonctionne pas : **un portage intégral de la couche data est obligatoire**, pas une option.

---

## 2. `crim50n/oc-remote` — alternative sobre

| Métrique | Valeur |
|---|---|
| HEAD | `3dd31a5` — 2026-09-06 (**stale 18 j**) |
| Fichiers `.kt` | 150 |
| Lignes Kotlin `main` | **39 099** |
| Tests | **57 fichiers**, 3 538 LOC (ratio test/main 3× meilleur que starburst) |
| Taille repo | 15 Mo |
| APK release v1.10.0 | **5,35 Mo** (pas de natif embarqué) |
| Stars / forks | **154 / 34** — vraie traction |
| Écrans / ViewModels | 15 / 11 |

Architecture : **MVVM + Hilt**, monomodule `:app`, même stack Compose BOM 2024.12.01 / Ktor 2.3.11 / markdown-renderer 0.28.0 que starburst (lignée commune). `minSdk=26`, `targetSdk=34`, AGP 8.4.0, Kotlin 2.0.21.

Points notables :
- **`domain/model/PendingInteraction.kt`** : `sealed interface` propre `Permission | Question`, avec id+sessionId. C'est le modèle le plus clair des trois repos pour la file d'interactions.
- **`data/repository/EventReducer.kt`** (1 057 LOC) : réducteur d'événements structuré, avec tests (`EventReducerTest.kt`), + `PendingPromptRepository.kt`, `DraftRepository.kt`, `ServerConnectionStateRepository.kt` → gestion d'état offline/reconnexion sérieuse.
- **`SseClient.kt`** (612 LOC) lit `/global/event` (V1), mêmes noms d'événements V1 que starburst, mais ajoute `question.asked/replied/rejected` gérés proprement.
- `ChatScreen.kt` fait **9 069 LOC** (monolithe) et `ChatViewModel.kt` 1 867 LOC.
- Pas de STT, pas de TTS, pas de widget, pas de MNN/natif, pas de JSch. Plus sobre.
- **Même problème V1** : endpoints `/session`, `/permission`, `/question`, `/pty`, `/global/event`. Sa file permissions/questions est **réutilisable comme design**, pas comme code réseau.

---

## 3. `omnicus/opencode2-mobile` — la doc V2 vivante

Expo/RN, MIT, HEAD `13f9ffb` — 2026-09-24. Seul client **V2 réel**. Ne mesure pas la qualité, extrait la connaissance. Le cœur exploitable est `packages/opencode-adapter/src/index.ts` (**1 899 LOC**) qui pinne `@opencode/client@2.0.16`.

### Endpoints V2 réels (extraits du client officiel `@opencode/client@2.0.16`, extrait npm)

Tous les appels passent par la même forme. Extrait de `packages/opencode-adapter/src/index.ts` :

```ts
// Permission V2 — index.ts:645-653
export function replyOpenCodePermissionRequest(
  client, sessionID, requestID, reply: PermissionReply, options,
) {
  return client.permission.reply({ decision: reply, requestID, sessionID }, options);
}
// PermissionReply = "once" | "always" | "reject"  (types.d.ts:531)

// Form V2 — index.ts:680-698
client.session.form.reply({ answer, formID, sessionID }, options);
client.session.form.get({ formID, sessionID }, options);
client.session.form.cancel({ formID, sessionID }, options);

// Prompt V2 — index.ts:520-532
const inbox = await client.session.prompt({ ...input, sessionID }, options);
// input.id doit matcher /^msg_/ ; retour = SessionInboxInfo (pas un message)

// Création session — index.ts:468-483
client.session.create({ ...input, location: { directory, workspaceID? } }, options);
```

Chemins HTTP sous-jacents, extraits des chunks du client officiel (`path:` templates) :

```
GET    /api/event                                      <- SSE V2
GET    /api/info      GET /api/location   GET /api/project
GET    /api/agent     GET /api/command    GET /api/model    GET /api/config
GET    /api/skill     GET /api/vcs/status GET /api/vcs/diff
GET    /api/fs/list   GET /api/fs/read/{path}  GET /api/fs/find
GET    /api/session                POST /api/session
GET    /api/session/active
GET    /api/session/{sid}          DELETE /api/session/{sid}
GET    /api/session/{sid}/message  GET /api/session/{sid}/message/{mid}
POST   /api/session/{sid}/prompt
POST   /api/session/{sid}/agent    POST /api/session/{sid}/model
POST   /api/session/{sid}/interrupt  POST /api/session/{sid}/background
POST   /api/session/{sid}/command    POST /api/session/{sid}/fork
POST   /api/session/{sid}/compact    POST /api/session/{sid}/revert
GET    /api/session/{sid}/inbox      POST /api/session/{sid}/inbox/{inboxID}
GET    /api/permission/request       POST /api/session/{sid}/permission/{rid}/reply
GET    /api/form
GET    /api/session/{sid}/form/{fid}
POST   /api/session/{sid}/form/{fid}/reply
DELETE /api/session/{sid}/form/{fid}                  <- cancel
GET    /api/mcp  /api/provider  /api/shell  /api/worktree  /api/websearch
POST   /api/rpc/{rpcID}/{method}
```

**DTOs exacts (types.d.ts du client officiel)** :

```ts
PermissionRequest = { id, sessionID, action, resources: string[], save?: string[],
                      metadata?, source?, message? }          // types.d.ts:2235
PermissionReplyInput = { sessionID, requestID,
                         decision: "once"|"always"|"reject", message? }  // :7680
SessionFormReplyInput = { sessionID, formID,
                          answer: { [key]: string|number|boolean|string[] } }  // :6968
SessionPromptInput = { sessionID, id? (/^msg_/), text,
                       files?: {uri,name?,description?,mention?}[],
                       agents?, skills?, delivery?: "steer"|"queue", model? }   // :5369
SessionMessageInfo = AgentSelected | ModelSelected | LocationSwitched | User
                   | Synthetic | System | Skill | Shell | Assistant
                   | Compaction | Idle                              // :3247
```

**Enveloppes** : les listes renvoient `{ data: [...], cursor: { previous?, next? } }` ; `/api/location` renvoie `{ directory, project:{id,directory,canonical}, workspaceID? }`. Il y a un `location` partout (`?location[directory]=...` en query). Le prompt V2 n'est **pas** une réponse streamée : il renvoie un item d'inbox (`msg_xxx`), le stream arrive par `/api/event`.

### Noms d'événements SSE V2 (liste exhaustive extraite)

```
server.connected
permission.asked / permission.replied
form.created / form.replied / form.cancelled
session.created / updated / deleted / forked / moved / renamed
session.status / idle
session.execution.started / succeeded / failed / interrupted
session.step.started / ended / failed / streamed
session.text.started / delta / ended
session.reasoning.started / delta / ended
session.tool.input.started / delta / ended
session.tool.called / progress / success / failed
session.shell.started / ended
session.inbox.enqueued / delivered / cancelled / delivery.changed
session.message.content.updated      <- remplace message.part.updated V1
session.usage.recorded / updated
session.compaction.ended / failed
session.retry.scheduled / session.synthetic / session.viewed
```

**Différence structurante vs V1** : plus de `session.next.*` ni de `message.part.*`. Le contenu assistant V2 arrive sous forme de **liste typée encodée** : `data.content: Array<SessionMessageAssistantContentEncoded>` dans `session.message.content.updated`. Ce n'est plus « message + parts » comme en V1 (`MessageWithParts`/`Part` chez starburst et oc-remote).

### Notifications push self-hosted

Architecture `packages/opencode-notification-plugin` (plugin V2) → `apps/notification-broker` (broker loopback) → **Expo Push Service → APNs/FCM**. Le broker est **self-hosted** (CLI de pairing, challenge chiffré, `notification-protocol` 697 LOC), mais le dernier maillon est **FCM/APNs**.

**⚠️ Rédhibitoire pour GrapheneOS sans Play Services.** Et **aucune trace d'UnifiedPush ni de ntfy** dans tout le repo (grep sur `.ts/.tsx/.json/.md` : 0 résultat). À réutiliser : le **modèle** de sécurité du broker (pairing, texte catégorisé en allowlist finie, jamais de payload brut), pas le transport.

Le plugin V2 s'abonne à `permission.asked`, `permission.replied`, `form.created`, `form.replied`, `form.cancelled`, `session.execution.succeeded` — confirmation que ces événements existent côté serveur V2 et sont le bon point d'accroche pour un futur ntfy.
